name: Wendy Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I maintain a claims system that small insurance companies use, the software that tracks a burst pipe from the first phone call to the cheque. The company's about eighty people on a business park outside town, and the system's older than I am in places. Most days I'm in the database, working out why a claim from 2014 suddenly shows the wrong address. I like that it's steady and I know where everything lives; I don't like the weekend call-outs when a client's month-end report breaks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your life like away from the office?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a studio flat on my own, and I've got a ten-year-old hatchback on a loan because the business park has one bus an hour. The pay's below what developers get in the city, but the city's two hours away, and around here it's us or the hospital IT department. I've usually got about three weeks of money in the bank before payday, and that's on a good month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds about right to me, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected and leave it there. I'm not one for posting, but if someone at work brought it up I'd say tools come and go, the claims still need processing. I'd probably make a joke about all the meetings we had about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, but my worries are older than AI. The car loan runs another two years, and if the clutch goes I'm on a credit card. Our company lost a client last spring, and nobody's told us what that means yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep turning down the AI trial the team lead keeps offering. I'd try to pay the car loan off a few months early by doing more weekend call-outs, since they pay extra. And I'd start a small emergency fund, even forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer about AI, but the usual money worry stays. AI fading is like the weather getting better while the roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine parts of your work might AI still take, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the month-end reports, which are mostly copying numbers into a template. That's a day a month for me. I'd miss the overtime more than the work, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did losing that client last spring feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet, which was the worst part. Nobody was let go, but two contractors weren't renewed, and the coffee machine was taken away. You notice the little things.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**, and that tools **come and go** while claims still need doing.
I'd make a **joke** about all the meetings we had about AI.
think: My worries are **older than AI**: the car loan and a possible clutch repair.
Our company **lost a client** last spring, and nobody's explained what it means yet.
do: Keep turning down the **AI trial** the team lead keeps offering.
Pay the **car loan** off early by taking more weekend call-outs.
Start an **emergency fund**, even at forty a month.
feel: Calmer about AI, but with the usual **money worry**, like a **leaking roof**.
S0.quote: AI fading is like the weather getting better while the roof still leaks.
fieldNote: Her **money pressure** comes from the car loan and thin savings, not from AI.
The **lost client** and missing coffee machine show she reads small signs carefully.
She'd miss **overtime** pay more than the reporting task itself.

steps.text: Keep fixing claims database bugs without the AI trial
Take extra weekend call-outs to pay the car loan early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's the one where they actually make me use it, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use it for some things and not others, which is what I always say about everything. At work I'd go along with it, without being the first to sign up. I wouldn't be on the internet shouting either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the bit that saves me is the old database. Nobody else understands why the 2014 insurance claims are stored the way they are, and I don't think an AI will either, not quickly. But if they rebuild the whole system on something new, that protection is gone, and the rebuild is exactly what AI makes cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the AI training once it was required, and not before. I'd write down everything I know about the old database in a proper guide, so I'm the person who owns that knowledge. I'd cancel the streaming and the gym and put that money towards three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Like when a new manager starts and you don't know yet if they like you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Writing down what you know could make you easier to replace. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have, and it keeps me up a bit. But if I don't write it down, someone else will guess it with AI and get it wrong, and I'll be the one fixing it at midnight. I'd rather be the name on the guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at work is in the same spot as you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, who does the reports with me, and he's even less keen on change than I am. We have lunch in his car most days because the canteen's loud. If they rebuild the system, we're both in trouble.

say: I'd say AI is **sensible for some things**, not everything, and leave it there.
I'd **go along** with it at work without being the first to sign up.
think: My protection is the **old database**, which nobody else understands.
A full **rebuild** on new software would remove that protection, and AI makes rebuilds cheaper.
do: Take the **AI training** once it becomes required, not before.
Write a proper **guide** to the old database so the knowledge has her name on it.
Cancel streaming and the gym to build **three months** of savings.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, like a **new manager** whose view of her she doesn't know yet.
S1.quote: Nobody else understands why the 2014 insurance claims are stored the way they are, and I don't think an AI will either, not quickly.
fieldNote: She bets on **legacy knowledge** as her shield, and sees it could vanish with a rebuild.
Writing the **database guide** is a smart but nervous move she has already thought through.
Her lunch partner **Gareth** is in the same exposed spot.

steps.text: Take the required AI training course when the firm mandates it
Write a full guide to the old claims database
Save three months of expenses from the money freed up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's before my car's even paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and we'll all have to deal with it, and I'd hope the government has some sort of plan. I wouldn't rant. I'd just tell friends to hang on to cash and not sign up for anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished in that job within a year. If an AI can do any thinking work, it can read my old database faster than I can, guide or no guide. My whole job is a screen and a keyboard, so the robot delay doesn't buy me a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the weekend fun and put every spare penny towards the car loan, so at least I own the car. I'd ask the hospital IT department and the council about any jobs, even lower paid. If the worst happened I'd move back in with my mum and give up the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. I'm not someone who likes change, and this is all the change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would going back to your mum's be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a forty-minute drive and a box room with my old swimming medals on the wall. Mum would be lovely about it, which almost makes it worse. At twenty-seven I'd feel like I'd gone backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything hands-on you could see yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worked in my aunt's café through university, so maybe that, for a few years until robots can make a decent sandwich. I'd hate it after an office job. But a café is better than nothing in a town like ours.

say: I'd say it's **happening**, and hope the government has some sort of **plan**.
I'd tell friends to **hang on to cash** and not sign up for anything big.
think: I'd be **finished** in that job within a year, guide or no guide.
My job is a **screen and keyboard**, so the robot delay buys me nothing.
do: Put every spare penny towards the **car loan** so I own the car outright.
Ask the **hospital IT** department and the council about any jobs.
Move back to **Mum's** and give up the flat if the worst happens.
feel: **Sick** to her stomach, facing **all the change** at once.
S2.quote: My whole job is a screen and a keyboard, so the robot delay doesn't buy me a thing.
fieldNote: Her **legacy knowledge** shield collapses here, and she sees it at once.
Moving back to **Mum's box room** would feel like going backwards at 27.
Her fallback is her **aunt's café**, hands-on but plainly not wanted.

steps.text: Pay off the hatchback loan early with every spare penny
Apply to the hospital IT department and the council
Ask about shifts at her aunt's café
Give up the studio flat and move back to Mum's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it, but it's still quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan, not panic, and that employers should give people time to retrain. I'd vote for whoever had the most sensible plan, whichever side it came from. At work I'd ask the managers straight out what they expect the team to look like in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know I'm slow to move, so five years could disappear on me. I'd keep thinking there's time, and then suddenly it's 2030. The job will probably last three years and then get thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd pay off the car and get three months saved. Then I'd look at becoming a claims assessor, the person who visits flooded houses, because that's part people, part hands-on. My company's clients do that work, so I already know the forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, in a grinding way. Not panic, but it'd be sitting there every Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why claims assessor and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know the claims process from the inside. A flooded kitchen still needs someone to stand in it and talk to the owner. That holds at least until the robots in 2034. It's not perfect, but it's close to what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said time could disappear on you. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a deadline someone else sets, like a course start date I've paid for. I'm good once I've committed. It's the deciding I'm bad at.

say: I'd say we need a **proper plan**, not panic, and time to retrain.
I'd ask managers straight out what the **team looks like** in 2031.
think: I'm **slow to move**, so five years could vanish before I act.
The job probably **lasts three years** and then gets thinner.
do: Pay off the car and get **three months** saved in the first year.
Train as a **claims assessor** who visits flooded homes.
Pay up front for a course so a **fixed start date** forces me to move.
feel: A **grinding worry** that would sit there every **Sunday night**.
S3.quote: A flooded kitchen still needs someone to stand in it and talk to the owner.
fieldNote: Her **claims assessor** plan uses what she knows and adds a hands-on part.
She knows her own **slowness** is the biggest risk with five years.
She expects to **lose the job** within a few years, which keeps the mood alarmed.

steps.text: Pay off the car and save three months in year one
Book and pay for a claims assessor training course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Right. I could almost forget about that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. I'd tell people to keep calm and plan sensibly. I'd want the government to make retraining cheap rather than throw money around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be tempted to ignore it for five years, because that's what I'm like. The job's probably fine until about 2033. The real risk is me being forty-ish with nothing else lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job, pay off the car, and finally build three months of savings. Around year four I'd start the claims assessor training part-time. I'd probably also give in and learn the AI tools at work, because by then everyone would be using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, but it'd nag at me. It's the kind of thing you don't think about until you can't sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start earlier than year four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my colleague Gareth got let go first, I'd know AI is real, which I suppose is a terrible way to plan. He's even slower to change than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. My mum's nearby and I like it here. If the jobs go, they go everywhere, so moving to the city doesn't feel like it'd fix much.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so nobody should be caught out.
I'd want the government to make **retraining cheap** rather than throw money around.
think: I'd be tempted to **ignore it** for five years, because that's what I'm like.
The real risk is being **forty-ish** with nothing else lined up.
do: Keep doing the job, **pay off the car** and build three months of savings.
Start **claims assessor** training part-time around year four.
Learn the **AI tools** at work once everyone else is using them.
feel: Mostly okay, with a **nagging** worry that shows up when she **can't sleep**.
S4.quote: If my colleague Gareth got let go first, I'd know AI is real, which I suppose is a terrible way to plan.
fieldNote: She admits she'd wait for a **colleague to be cut** before moving.
Her **mum nearby** keeps her rooted, and she doubts moving would help.
Job looks fine **until about 2033**, but her delay habit keeps her anxious.

steps.text: Pay off the car and build three months of savings
Start part-time claims assessor training around year four
Learn the AI tools once colleagues all use them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough for someone like me who takes a year to decide what phone to buy. What would help is a proper redundancy payment, enough to cover six months, and cheap courses at the local college for jobs that still need people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how small towns are different. In the city there are fifty firms; here there's my firm and the hospital, and if both go, that's it. In the city you just move to another one.

headlineQuote: In the city there are fifty firms; here there's my firm and the hospital, and if both go, that's it.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old** developer maintaining an old insurance claims system on a business park.
She lives alone, pays off a **car loan**, and has about three weeks of savings.
She never uses AI and relies on **legacy knowledge** nobody else has.
Her mood rises from uneasy to **alarmed** once AGI makes that knowledge worthless.
Her plan is to become a **claims assessor**, if she can push herself to start.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she takes a year to decide anything and two years is too short.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap college courses** for jobs that still need people.
